bridges-6-a-explanation: Bridges are in the early stages of development and the optimal design likely has not been discovered yet. Many of the largest hacks in blockchain history have involved bridges.
payments-1-prompt: Why would someone living with high inflation choose to save in stablecoins?
payments-1-a-label: Stablecoins are usually tied to strong currencies like the US Dollar, so savings hold their value
payments-1-a-explanation: Earning and saving in stablecoins lets people preserve, or even grow, purchasing power while their local currency depreciates.
payments-1-b-label: Their local central bank issues and guarantees the stablecoin
payments-1-b-explanation: Stablecoins are part of an alternative financial system that is independent of any nation's monetary policies or control.
payments-1-c-label: Stablecoins pay a fixed interest rate set by the Ethereum network
payments-1-c-explanation: Stablecoins are built for steady value, not a set return. The network pays no interest on them.
payments-1-d-label: Stablecoins can only be spent online, not with local businesses
payments-1-d-explanation: Stablecoins make payments for goods and services easier both locally and globally.
payments-2-prompt: What does a person need in order to receive an Ethereum payment from abroad?
payments-2-a-label: A bank account in the country the money is sent from
payments-2-a-explanation: No bank account is involved. This is why Ethereum reaches people in regions with limited banking infrastructure.
payments-2-b-label: Approval from a remittance service during its business hours
payments-2-b-explanation: Ethereum is a global, 24/7 platform, so a payment never waits on a service's opening hours.
payments-2-c-label: An internet connection and a wallet app
payments-2-c-explanation: An internet connection and a wallet app are all it takes to send or receive ether.
payments-2-d-label: A local agent to hand over the cash in person
payments-2-d-explanation: Nothing changes hands in person. The funds land directly in the recipient's wallet, wherever they are.
payments-3-prompt: How does a self-custodial crypto card differ from a custodial one?
payments-3-a-label: It can only be used at shops that accept crypto directly
payments-3-a-explanation: These cards run on the Visa and Mastercard networks, so they work for everyday spending like coffee, groceries, or a flight.
payments-3-b-label: You keep control of your assets instead of depositing them with a third party
payments-3-b-explanation: Custodial cards require you to deposit funds with a third party first; self-custodial cards spend straight from your own wallet or smart contract account.
payments-3-c-label: Your private keys are stored with the card issuer for safekeeping
payments-3-c-explanation: Handing keys to an issuer would put a middleman back in control, which is the opposite of self-custody.
payments-3-d-label: It converts your crypto into a bank balance you spend later
payments-3-d-explanation: No bank holds the balance. Your assets stay under your own onchain control until the moment you spend.
payments-4-prompt: You open a news article and, instead of a paywall, the site asks for the few cents it costs to unlock it. Under the x402 standard, what happens next?
payments-4-a-label: The visitor is asked to create an account and start a subscription
payments-4-a-explanation: x402 exists so a single action can be paid for directly, with no account, subscription, or API key.
payments-4-b-label: The request is blocked until the visitor buys ETH to cover gas
payments-4-b-explanation: The payer only needs one of the supported stablecoins. No ETH for gas is required.
payments-4-c-label: The server charges the visitor's stored card details
payments-4-c-explanation: No card is involved. Payment comes from the payer's own wallet.
payments-4-d-label: The wallet handles the payment, with one click or automatically from a pre-approved allowance
payments-4-d-explanation: Wallets, and AI agents with pre-approved balances, can detect the price and pay instantly to unlock the resource.
payments-5-prompt: Ethereum payments are untraceable because no bank is involved.
payments-5-a-explanation: By default, transactions are recorded on a public ledger anyone can verify, which is how a charity can prove where donations went. Privacy techniques can hide a transfer's details while keeping the ledger verifiable, but skipping the bank does not by itself hide anything.
payments-6-prompt: Ethereum payments can be programmable. What does that make possible?
payments-6-a-label: Transfers arrive in minutes no matter where the two people are
payments-6-a-explanation: True of Ethereum, but that is settlement speed, not programmability.
payments-6-b-label: Anyone with an internet connection can be paid
payments-6-b-explanation: True of Ethereum, but that is open access, not programmability.
payments-6-c-label: Funds can be released automatically once agreed conditions are met
payments-6-c-explanation: Smart contracts are self-enforcing agreements: the terms are written into code, and the code holds the parties to them. That supports escrow, recurring payments, and performance-based compensation.
payments-6-d-label: An authority can step in and adjust the money supply
payments-6-d-explanation: That describes central bank policy. Ethereum's issuance is predictable and no authority adjusts it.
blocks-1-prompt: Why does Ethereum group transactions into blocks instead of committing each one on its own?
blocks-1-a-label: It gives everyone on the network enough time to agree on the same history
blocks-1-a-explanation: Spacing out commits lets all participants reach consensus, so they hold a synchronized state and agree on the precise history of transactions.
blocks-1-b-label: It keeps transaction contents hidden until the block is published
blocks-1-b-explanation: Blocks are a synchronization tool, not a privacy one. Batching exists so the whole network can commit and agree on the same transactions at once.
blocks-1-c-label: It compresses transactions so they take up less space on the chain
blocks-1-c-explanation: Batching is about agreement, not size. A block commits dozens or hundreds of transactions all at once so the network stays in sync.
blocks-1-d-label: Ethereum can only process one transaction at a time, so they wait in line
blocks-1-d-explanation: Transaction requests arrive dozens of times per second, and a single block commits dozens or hundreds of them together.
blocks-2-prompt: What makes it impractical to quietly edit a transaction in a block from last year?
blocks-2-a-label: Blocks become locked by the protocol once they reach a certain age
blocks-2-a-explanation: Nothing locks a block by age. Tampering is caught because a block's hash (a fingerprint of its data, which includes the previous block's hash) changes the moment anything is edited.
blocks-2-b-label: Every block carries a hash of the block before it, so an edit would invalidate every block that follows
blocks-2-b-explanation: Hashes are cryptographically derived from block data, so one change anywhere in history invalidates all the following blocks and everyone running the blockchain notices.
blocks-2-c-label: Block contents are encrypted, so nobody can read or change them
blocks-2-c-explanation: Hashing is not encryption, and block data is public for anyone to inspect. The chain resists tampering because any edit breaks the hashes everyone else can check.
blocks-2-d-label: The Ethereum Foundation keeps a reference copy of the chain to compare against
blocks-2-d-explanation: No single party holds an authoritative copy. Every participant running the blockchain would see the broken hashes for themselves.
blocks-3-prompt: Under proof-of-stake, who builds the next block?
blocks-3-a-label: Whichever validator's hardware solves the block's puzzle first
blocks-3-a-explanation: That is proof-of-work. Proof-of-stake has no race to solve anything: one validator is selected per slot.
blocks-3-b-label: Whichever validator bids the most ETH for the slot
blocks-3-b-explanation: Slots are not auctioned. Staked ETH is collateral against bad behavior, not a bid for block production.
blocks-3-c-label: A committee that ETH holders vote into place
blocks-3-c-explanation: There is no election. A validator is randomly selected for each slot.
blocks-3-d-label: A validator selected at random for that slot, with at least 32 ETH staked as collateral
blocks-3-d-explanation: In every twelve-second slot a randomly selected validator bundles transactions, executes them, determines the new state, and passes the block around. Validators stake at least 32 ETH, which they can lose if they act dishonestly or fail to keep up their duties.
blocks-4-prompt: A node receives a new block. How does it decide the block is valid?
blocks-4-a-label: It trusts the proposer's signature, since the proposer has ETH at risk
blocks-4-a-explanation: Stake discourages dishonesty, but it does not replace verification. Every other validator re-executes the transactions itself.
blocks-4-b-label: It accepts the block once most other nodes have accepted it
blocks-4-b-explanation: Nodes do not take each other's word for it. Each one re-executes the block's transactions and checks the result independently.
blocks-4-c-label: It re-executes the block's transactions and checks that the resulting state matches the state_root recorded in the block
blocks-4-c-explanation: Clients re-execute the transactions in the execution_payload and compare the state they get against the state_root in the block. A match means the block is valid and safe to add.
blocks-4-d-label: It checks that every transaction in the block paid enough gas
blocks-4-d-explanation: Paying for gas does not make a block valid. Validity comes from re-executing the transactions and arriving at the state the block claims.
blocks-5-prompt: Ethereum produces a new block every twelve seconds, without exception.
blocks-5-a-explanation: Time is divided into twelve-second slots with one validator selected to propose in each, so twelve seconds is the expected block time. But a validator that is offline when its turn comes leaves that slot empty and no block is produced.
blocks-6-prompt: Why does Ethereum limit how much gas a single block can use?
blocks-6-a-label: To cap how much ETH can move in one block
blocks-6-a-explanation: The limit applies to gas, the computation a block performs, not to the value it transfers.
blocks-6-b-label: To give each validator an equal quota, so no proposer can include more transactions than another
blocks-6-b-explanation: The limit is per block, not a per-validator quota. The total gas used by all transactions in a block must stay under it.
blocks-6-c-label: Because block size is fixed in the protocol and cannot be changed
blocks-6-c-explanation: It is not fixed. Blocks have a target size and can grow toward a hard limit of twice that target as demand rises, and validators can nudge the limit up or down by a small factor each block through consensus.
blocks-6-d-label: Because blocks could otherwise grow so large that less powerful nodes fall behind
blocks-6-d-explanation: Larger blocks need more space and more computing power to process in time for the next slot. Arbitrarily large blocks would gradually push less performant full nodes off the network, a centralizing force the cap resists.
accounts-1-prompt: Which statement about contract accounts is true?
accounts-1-a-label: The developer who deployed the contract holds its private key
accounts-1-a-explanation: Contract accounts don't have private keys. They are controlled by the logic of the smart contract code.
accounts-1-b-label: Contract accounts can't receive or send ETH, only run code
accounts-1-b-explanation: Both account types can receive, hold, and send ETH and tokens.
accounts-1-c-label: A contract account can only perform actions in response to receiving a transaction
accounts-1-c-explanation: Contract code runs when the account receives a message call, so a transaction has to trigger it first.
accounts-1-d-label: Deploying a contract account is free, just like creating an externally-owned account
accounts-1-d-explanation: Creating an externally-owned account costs nothing, but deploying a contract has a cost because you're using network storage.
accounts-2-prompt: An account's nonce counts the transactions it has sent. What does that counter protect against?
accounts-2-a-label: Spending more ETH than the account holds
accounts-2-a-explanation: The balance field records the wei owned by the address. The nonce only counts transactions sent or contracts created.
accounts-2-b-label: The same signed transaction being broadcast and executed again
accounts-2-b-explanation: Only one transaction with a given nonce can be executed for each account, which blocks replay attacks.
accounts-2-c-label: Someone working out the account's private key
accounts-2-c-explanation: Private keys stay safe because key derivation only runs one way, not because of the nonce.
accounts-2-d-label: A deployed contract's code being altered
accounts-2-d-explanation: The codeHash field cannot be changed, unlike the other account fields. That immutability doesn't come from the nonce.
accounts-3-prompt: Why does your private key matter so much?
accounts-3-a-label: It's the address you share with people so they can pay you
accounts-3-a-explanation: The address you share is public, derived from your public key. The private key is the half you never share.
accounts-3-b-label: It's stored on Ethereum so the network can confirm your balance
accounts-3-b-explanation: Private keys are never published to the network. Others verify a transaction by deriving your public key from its signature.
accounts-3-c-label: It holds your ether, so if the key is gone the ETH is gone from the network too
accounts-3-c-explanation: Funds are always recorded on Ethereum's ledger. The key is what grants access to them.
accounts-3-d-label: It digitally signs transactions, which is what gives you custody of the account's funds
accounts-3-d-explanation: You never really hold cryptocurrency, you hold private keys. Signing proves a transaction came from you.
accounts-4-prompt: Anyone who knows your Ethereum address can work backwards from it to your private key.
accounts-4-a-explanation: The public key is generated from the private key, and the address from the public key. You can derive new public keys from a private key, but you cannot derive a private key from public keys.
accounts-5-prompt: A new contract is deployed. Where does its address come from?
accounts-5-a-label: The creator's address, combined with either that account's nonce or a chosen salt and a hash of the contract's code
accounts-5-a-explanation: Ethereum has two deployment schemes. CREATE uses the creator's address and nonce, while CREATE2 uses the creator's address, a salt they pick, and a hash of the contract's creation code.
accounts-5-b-label: The developer picks it while writing the contract
accounts-5-b-explanation: The address is worked out at deployment from the creator's address and other inputs; it isn't set in the source code.
accounts-5-c-label: The contract shares the address of the account that deployed it
accounts-5-c-explanation: A contract gets its own address. The creator's address is only one of the inputs used to compute it.
accounts-5-d-label: It's generated from a random private key, the same way an externally-owned account is
accounts-5-d-explanation: Contract accounts have no private keys, and their addresses are computed rather than random.
accounts-6-prompt: How does a wallet relate to an Ethereum account?
accounts-6-a-label: The wallet is the account, so switching wallets means starting a new account
accounts-6-a-explanation: An account is not a wallet. The same account can be reached through different wallets.
accounts-6-b-label: The wallet is where your ETH is stored
accounts-6-b-explanation: A balance is a field of the account on Ethereum's ledger. A wallet is the interface you use to read that account and, when it holds your keys, to sign transactions for it.
accounts-6-c-label: The wallet is an interface or application you use to interact with your account
accounts-6-c-explanation: Wallets work with either account type, externally-owned or contract.
accounts-6-d-label: You have to set up a wallet contract before an account can hold ETH
accounts-6-d-explanation: Externally-owned accounts cost nothing to create and can receive, hold, and send ETH and tokens on their own.
accounts-7-prompt: What do you need in order to create an externally-owned account?
accounts-7-a-label: Approval from a node operator or validator
accounts-7-a-explanation: No one grants you an account. A wallet or library generates the key pair on your own machine, and the network learns the address only when it's used.
accounts-7-b-label: An identity document linking the account to you
accounts-7-b-explanation: Unlike with a bank account, no documents or approval are involved. Your address is derived from your public key, and nothing about you is collected.
accounts-7-c-label: A small amount of ETH to cover the account's storage
accounts-7-c-explanation: Creating an externally-owned account costs nothing. Deploying a contract account has a cost because it uses network storage.
accounts-7-d-label: A randomly generated private key, which wallets or libraries will produce for you
accounts-7-d-explanation: That key is all an account is: the public key comes from it, and the address is the last 20 bytes of the public key's Keccak-256 hash.
energy-consumption-1-prompt: Under proof-of-stake, what does Ethereum use to secure the network in place of large amounts of energy?
energy-consumption-1-a-explanation: Ethereum's proof-of-stake consensus mechanism uses ETH, rather than energy, to secure the network.
energy-consumption-1-b-explanation: Mining hardware is what proof-of-work needed: miners ran hardware to calculate a value, spending energy in the process. Ethereum no longer works this way.
energy-consumption-1-c-label: Carbon offsets bought by the Ethereum Foundation
energy-consumption-1-c-explanation: Ethereum's route to sustainability was to replace the energy-hungry part of the network with a green alternative, not to offset emissions.
energy-consumption-1-d-label: Renewable energy contracts signed by node operators
energy-consumption-1-d-explanation: Ethereum's energy use is low because of how consensus works, not because of where node operators get their electricity.
energy-consumption-2-prompt: Compared with the Bitcoin network, proof-of-stake Ethereum's estimated annual energy use is:
energy-consumption-2-a-label: About the same, since both are blockchains
energy-consumption-2-a-explanation: Being a blockchain does not set a network's energy use; the consensus mechanism does. July 2023 estimates put Bitcoin at ~149 TWh/yr against ~0.0026 TWh/yr for Ethereum.
energy-consumption-2-b-explanation: The gap is far wider: roughly 53,000 times. July 2023 estimates put Bitcoin at ~149 TWh/yr and proof-of-stake Ethereum at ~0.0026 TWh/yr.
energy-consumption-2-c-label: Tens of thousands of times smaller
energy-consumption-2-c-explanation: July 2023 estimates put Bitcoin at ~149 TWh/yr and proof-of-stake Ethereum at ~0.0026 TWh/yr, around 53,000 times less.
energy-consumption-2-d-label: Larger, because Ethereum handles more transactions per second
energy-consumption-2-d-explanation: Higher throughput does not raise Ethereum's energy use: the energy to propose and validate a block is the same whatever the block holds. Its estimate sits far below Bitcoin's.
energy-consumption-3-prompt: Reducing the number of transactions in Ethereum's blocks would lower the network's energy use.
energy-consumption-3-a-explanation: The energy needed to propose and validate a block is independent of how many transactions it holds, which is why per-transaction energy figures are misleading.
energy-consumption-4-prompt: Ethereum's move from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake changed its annual electricity use by how much?
energy-consumption-4-a-explanation: The drop was far larger. CCRI estimates The Merge (transition to proof-of-stake) cut Ethereum's annualized electricity consumption by more than 99.988%.
energy-consumption-4-b-explanation: Still far short of the real figure: more than 99.988%.
energy-consumption-4-c-explanation: CCRI estimates The Merge (transition to proof-of-stake) reduced Ethereum's annualized electricity consumption by more than 99.988%.
energy-consumption-4-d-label: It barely changed, because validators still run hardware on the network
energy-consumption-4-d-explanation: Validators do run nodes, but they no longer spend energy calculating values the way miners did. Measured electricity use fell by more than 99.988%.
energy-consumption-5-prompt: What does the regenerative finance (ReFi) community build on Ethereum?
energy-consumption-5-a-label: A protocol upgrade that cuts validator energy use further
energy-consumption-5-a-explanation: ReFi is built on Ethereum's application layer. It does not change how the network reaches consensus.
energy-consumption-5-b-label: A carbon accounting standard run by the Ethereum Foundation
energy-consumption-5-b-explanation: ReFi is an open, growing community of builders, not a Foundation program.
energy-consumption-5-c-label: Rules requiring applications to prove they run on renewable energy
energy-consumption-5-c-explanation: ReFi is about applications that benefit the environment, not restrictions on how Ethereum is run.
energy-consumption-5-d-label: Financial applications whose side effects benefit the environment
energy-consumption-5-d-explanation: ReFi applications use DeFi components to build financial applications with positive externalities for the environment.
how-ethereum-works-description: A closer look at the machinery of the network itself, from accounts and transactions to the software that keeps Ethereum running.
evm-1-prompt: The EVM is one machine, running in one place, that Ethereum nodes send their transactions to for execution.
evm-1-a-explanation: Nothing is sent off to a central machine. Every Ethereum node runs its own instance of the EVM to execute the transactions it receives, and because the EVM is deterministic, each one arrives at the same result.
evm-2-prompt: Bitcoin is usually described as a distributed ledger. Why is that description not enough for Ethereum?
evm-2-a-label: Ethereum has no native currency of its own
evm-2-a-explanation: Ethereum has its own native cryptocurrency, ether, which follows almost exactly the same rules a ledger-based currency does.
evm-2-b-label: Ethereum stores files and documents instead of transactions
evm-2-b-explanation: Contracts can hold arbitrary data in their storage, but as state rather than as files. A transaction is a change to that state, much as a Bitcoin transaction is a change to the ledger.
evm-2-c-label: Ethereum's rules let an account spend more than it has received
evm-2-c-explanation: Ether follows almost exactly the same intuitive rules as Bitcoin, including that an account cannot spend what it never received.
evm-2-d-label: Ethereum's state also holds a machine state that can execute arbitrary code
evm-2-d-explanation: Ethereum is better described as a distributed state transition machine: its state holds accounts and balances plus a machine state that can run arbitrary code and change from block to block.
evm-3-prompt: Ethereum can be described formally as having a state transition function. What does that function do?
evm-3-a-label: It applies transactions in a random order until the state balances
evm-3-a-explanation: The EVM behaves like a mathematical function: the same input always produces the same output, with nothing left to chance.
evm-3-b-label: It rebuilds the entire state from the first block each time
evm-3-b-explanation: A new state is produced by applying transactions to the previous valid state, not by starting over.
evm-3-c-label: It takes a valid old state and a set of valid transactions, and produces one new valid state
evm-3-c-explanation: Given an old valid state and a set of valid transactions, the state transition function produces one new valid state.
evm-3-d-label: It updates the state continuously as each transaction arrives, independently of blocks
evm-3-d-explanation: Ethereum's machine state changes from block to block, according to rules defined by the EVM.
evm-4-prompt: Ethereum has two kinds of transactions. What separates them?
evm-4-a-label: One results in a message call, the other creates a contract
evm-4-a-explanation: Contract creation deploys a new contract account holding compiled bytecode; a message call to that account executes the bytecode.
evm-4-b-label: One is signed by the sender, the other is submitted anonymously
evm-4-b-explanation: Every transaction is a cryptographically signed instruction from an account.
evm-4-c-label: One sends ether, the other sends gas
evm-4-c-explanation: Gas measures the computational effort an operation requires. It is not something you send to someone.
evm-4-d-label: One is executed by every node, the other only by the contract's author
evm-4-d-explanation: Nodes run the EVM to execute smart contracts, no matter who deployed them.
evm-5-prompt: A contract writes a value while handling a transaction. Where does that value have to live for a later transaction to read it?
evm-5-a-explanation: Memory is transient. It does not persist between transactions.
evm-5-b-explanation: A contract's storage is a Merkle Patricia trie tied to its account and part of the global state, so it persists.
evm-5-c-label: In transient storage, using the TSTORE opcode
evm-5-c-explanation: Transient storage stays available across the internal calls of one transaction, then is cleared when that transaction ends.
evm-5-d-explanation: The stack holds the 256-bit words an operation works on while code runs. Only the contract's storage trie becomes part of the global state.
evm-6-prompt: Execution clients ship EVM implementations written in Python, C++, JavaScript, and Rust. What keeps them all producing the same results?
evm-6-a-label: They are all compiled from one shared codebase
evm-6-a-explanation: Each implementation is written separately, in its own language.
evm-6-b-label: Nodes compare their results and take a majority vote whenever implementations disagree
evm-6-b-explanation: Agreement comes from implementing one shared specification, not from voting on outputs afterwards.
evm-6-c-label: Every implementation must follow the specification in the Ethereum Yellowpaper
evm-6-c-explanation: All implementations of the EVM must adhere to the specification described in the Ethereum Yellowpaper.
evm-6-d-label: The EVM's rules have never changed, so there is nothing to keep in sync
evm-6-d-explanation: The EVM has gone through several revisions over Ethereum's history, and implementations have to track the specification as it changes.
transactions-1-prompt: Who or what can send an Ethereum transaction?
transactions-1-a-label: Any node on the network, acting on the user's behalf
transactions-1-a-explanation: Any node can broadcast a request for a transaction to be executed, but it cannot originate one. The transaction has to be signed by the account it comes from.
transactions-1-b-label: An externally-owned account, the kind of account a private key controls
transactions-1-b-explanation: Transactions are cryptographically signed instructions from accounts, and every one has to be signed by the private key of an externally-owned account.
transactions-1-c-label: A smart contract, whenever the conditions written into it are met
transactions-1-c-explanation: Contract accounts cannot send transactions. A contract only runs when a transaction from an externally-owned account calls it. Even a Type 4 transaction, where an account delegates its authority to a contract, is still signed and sent by the account itself.
transactions-1-d-label: A validator, which writes the transactions it puts into a block
transactions-1-d-explanation: Validators execute transactions and propagate the resulting state change. They do not author them.
transactions-2-prompt: A transaction calls a function on a contract. How does the contract know which function to run?
transactions-2-a-label: The first four bytes of the data field identify the function
transactions-2-a-explanation: The selector is a hash of the function's name and arguments. The rest of the calldata is the arguments, encoded as the ABI specifies.
transactions-2-b-label: The function name travels with the transaction as readable text
transactions-2-b-explanation: The data field is hexadecimal, not text. The function is identified by a four-byte selector.
transactions-2-c-label: The recipient address points at the specific function being called
transactions-2-c-explanation: The recipient address identifies the contract. Which of its functions runs is decided by the data field.
transactions-2-d-label: The validator picks the function that matches the transaction's value
transactions-2-d-explanation: Validators execute what the transaction specifies. They make no choices about which code runs.
transactions-3-prompt: A wallet shows “Swap 1000 USDC for at least 0.25 WETH” before you sign. Where does that plain-language summary come from?
transactions-3-a-label: The wallet decrypts the transaction so its contents can be read
transactions-3-a-explanation: Transaction data is not encrypted, it is opaque hexadecimal. The problem is reading it, not unlocking it.
transactions-3-b-label: The validator inspects the transaction and reports what it will do
transactions-3-b-explanation: Validators execute transactions once they are signed and submitted. They tell the user nothing beforehand.
transactions-3-c-label: The wallet infers the likely intent from your past transactions
transactions-3-c-explanation: Nothing is inferred. The summary is built from that transaction's own data.
transactions-3-d-label: A transaction descriptor tells the wallet how to format the transaction's data
transactions-3-d-explanation: Descriptors defined by ERC-7730 map transaction variables into formatting templates, so a wallet can resolve token addresses into tickers and amounts into decimals and show what you are actually signing.
transactions-4-prompt: A transaction is sent with no recipient address. What is it doing?
transactions-4-a-label: Deploying a contract, with the contract's code carried in the data field
transactions-4-a-explanation: A contract deployment transaction has no recipient. The data field holds the code being deployed.
transactions-4-b-label: Destroying the ETH it carries, since there is no account to receive it
transactions-4-b-explanation: A missing recipient is not a burn. It signals that the transaction is creating a contract.
transactions-4-c-label: Nothing, the network rejects any transaction without a recipient
transactions-4-c-explanation: Transactions with no recipient address are valid, and they are how contracts get onto Ethereum in the first place.
transactions-4-d-label: Sending value back to the sender's own account
transactions-4-d-explanation: A transfer to yourself still needs a recipient address. Leaving the field out means something else entirely.
transactions-5-prompt: Bob pays a gas fee to send Alice 1 ETH. Where does that fee end up?
transactions-5-a-label: Entirely with the validator that included the transaction
transactions-5-a-explanation: The validator keeps only the priority fee tip. The larger base fee portion is burned.
transactions-5-b-label: With the company that operates the Ethereum network
transactions-5-b-explanation: No company runs Ethereum or collects its fees. The fee is either burned or paid to a validator as a tip.
transactions-5-c-label: The base fee is burned and the validator keeps the priority fee
transactions-5-c-explanation: Burning removes the base fee from circulation, and the tip is the validator's. Bob pays only for the gas his transaction actually used; the ETH set aside for the rest is refunded to his account.
transactions-5-d-label: Held by the network and returned to Bob once his block is finalized
transactions-5-d-explanation: The fee is a real cost, not a deposit. The only ETH Bob gets back is what was set aside for gas his transaction never used.
transactions-6-prompt: Reading a value out of a smart contract always costs gas.
transactions-6-a-explanation: Functions marked view or pure do not change a contract's state, so calling one from your own account costs no gas. Those same functions do cost gas when a contract calls them internally.
transactions-7-prompt: A validator has just included your transaction in a block. What makes it increasingly certain the transaction will never be undone?
transactions-7-a-label: It waits in the transaction pool until the rest of the network accepts it
transactions-7-a-explanation: The pool holds pending transactions before they are picked up. Once yours is in a block, that stage is behind it.
transactions-7-b-label: You can still cancel it for a short window, and that window closing settles it
transactions-7-b-explanation: There is no cancellation window. Certainty comes from the block itself being upgraded.
transactions-7-c-label: The block containing it is upgraded to “justified” and then “finalized”
transactions-7-c-explanation: Once a block is finalized, undoing it would take a network level attack that destroys an enormous amount of staked ETH.
transactions-7-d-label: Nothing further, inclusion in a block is already the final word
transactions-7-d-explanation: Inclusion makes a transaction successful, but the stronger guarantee arrives later, when the block is justified and then finalized.

ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-prompt: What is the main difference in purpose between Bitcoin and Ethereum?
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-a-label: Bitcoin is built for peer-to-peer payments; Ethereum is programmable, so it also runs applications
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-a-explanation: Ether moves peer-to-peer just as bitcoin does. The difference is scope: Ethereum is programmable, so the same network also runs apps from DeFi and stablecoins to NFTs and games.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-b-label: Ethereum is a faster copy of Bitcoin, controlled by the Ethereum Foundation
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-b-explanation: Ethereum was designed to do more than record payments, and it's not just about speed. And like Bitcoin, no single organization controls the protocol.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-c-label: Bitcoin is for institutions; Ethereum is for individuals
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-c-explanation: Anyone can use either network. The difference is what each is designed to do, not who it's for.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-d-label: They serve exactly the same purpose and compete directly
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-1-d-explanation: For many users the two networks are not in direct competition: they serve different purposes and can complement each other.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-prompt: Which consensus mechanisms do Bitcoin and Ethereum use today?
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-a-label: Both are mined, using energy-intensive proof-of-work
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-a-explanation: Ethereum stopped mining in 2022 when it switched to proof-of-stake, an upgrade known as The Merge. Only Bitcoin still uses mining.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-b-label: Bitcoin uses proof-of-work; Ethereum uses proof-of-stake
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-b-explanation: Bitcoin miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles. Ethereum validators instead stake ETH for the chance to propose blocks and risk losing it if they act dishonestly, a far greener design that needs no mining.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-c-explanation: Bitcoin still uses proof-of-work, where miners compete to solve puzzles and earn block rewards. Ethereum's proof-of-stake needs no mining and uses a negligible amount of energy by comparison.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-d-label: Bitcoin uses proof-of-stake; Ethereum uses proof-of-work
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-2-d-explanation: It's the reverse: Bitcoin has always used proof-of-work, and Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake in 2022.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-prompt: How do Bitcoin's and Ethereum's coin supplies differ?
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-a-label: Both have a fixed cap of 21 million coins
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-a-explanation: Only Bitcoin has the 21 million cap. Ether is uncapped by design: a small, ongoing issuance ensures validators are rewarded for securing the network in perpetuity.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-b-label: Ethereum has a fixed cap; Bitcoin's supply is unlimited
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-b-explanation: It's the reverse: Bitcoin caps at 21 million, while ether has no fixed cap.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-c-label: Bitcoin caps at 21 million coins; ether has no fixed cap, but fee burning can shrink its supply when activity is high
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-c-explanation: Since the London Upgrade (EIP-1559), part of every Ethereum transaction fee is burned. When network activity is high, more ETH can be burned than issued.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-d-label: Neither network places any limits on its supply
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-3-d-explanation: Both follow strict protocol rules: Bitcoin's cap is fixed at 21 million, and Ethereum's rate of issuance is set by the protocol according to how much ETH is staked.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-prompt: What is Ethereum's core innovation compared to Bitcoin?
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-a-label: Smart contracts: programs anyone can deploy, that run exactly as written
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-a-explanation: Smart contracts made the blockchain programmable, enabling apps for lending, trading, games, and digital collectibles that run every day for millions of users.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-b-explanation: Both networks let you send and receive value without a central authority. That was Bitcoin's original innovation.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-c-explanation: A fixed 21 million supply is Bitcoin's design, not Ethereum's.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-4-d-explanation: Neither network offers anonymity. Both record all transactions on a public ledger.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-5-prompt: Bitcoin and Ethereum consume roughly the same amount of energy.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-5-a-explanation: Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof-of-stake (The Merge) reduced its energy consumption by more than 99 percent. Bitcoin continues to use proof-of-work, which requires large amounts of electricity.
ethereum-vs-bitcoin-5-b-explanation: Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof-of-stake (The Merge) reduced its energy consumption by more than 99 percent. Bitcoin continues to use proof-of-work, which requires large amounts of electricity.
